title: Name tiers for recognizable working needs
trigger: Plan names express prestige but do not help visitors identify which capacity or workflow they need.
action: Pair each existing tier with a short fit statement tied to a verified job or scale, such as “For one client workspace” or “For teams managing several clients.” Keep the actual limits next to that statement.
mechanism: Self-recognition may make a tier easier to choose than an abstract good-better-best ladder.
guardrail: Do not invent audience restrictions or imply a smaller plan lacks shared capabilities; validate the fit statement against real limits.
measure: Paid plan selection; immediate plan changes and fit-related refunds.

title: Explain the incremental package at a glance
trigger: Each pricing card repeats a long feature list, obscuring what the higher tier adds.
action: Use “Everything in Starter, plus…” followed by the few verified additions that explain the price step. Retain an accessible complete comparison so buyers can confirm the shared foundation without rereading every card.
mechanism: Reduced repetition may focus attention on the decision-relevant difference.
guardrail: Check inherited features and exceptions; do not use the shorthand if the higher package removes or changes a lower-tier entitlement.
measure: Qualified upgrades at purchase; mistaken-feature support requests.

title: Order comparison rows by buying decisions
trigger: A feature matrix follows engineering or release order instead of the criteria buyers use to choose.
action: Reorder the first rows around the most frequent verified purchase questions, such as workload capacity, collaboration and required integrations. Group implementation details lower in the table with expandable explanations.
mechanism: Relevant early comparisons may reduce the effort needed to find a suitable plan.
guardrail: Use customer evidence or a stated hypothesis; retain material exclusions and avoid hiding an inconvenient differentiator below the fold.
measure: Plan-selection completion; missing-feature objections after purchase.

title: Quantify the actual capacity step
trigger: A larger plan claims “more” or “advanced” without making its capacity advantage intelligible.
action: Show the exact incremental capacity or ratio beside the two real limits, for example “40 active projects—4× Starter’s capacity.” Keep the price relationship separate so buyers can judge the trade-off rather than infer unlimited value.
mechanism: Concrete contrast may make an upgrade’s usable benefit easier to recognize.
guardrail: Compare the same unit and reset period; do not turn capacity into guaranteed completed work or hide a different limiting factor.
measure: Higher-tier paid selection; capacity utilization and downgrades.

title: Translate feature names into buyer consequences
trigger: The matrix contains internal labels such as custom roles or audit logs that target buyers do not understand.
action: Add a one-sentence explanation to each decisive technical feature, connecting it to the actual job: “Choose who may publish changes.” Keep the precise feature name available for technical evaluators.
mechanism: Concrete consequences may make unfamiliar capabilities relevant to a purchase decision.
guardrail: Describe implemented behavior accurately; do not inflate a convenience feature into a compliance or security certification.
measure: Qualified plan selection; feature-comprehension task success and support.

title: Offer a differences-only comparison view
trigger: A long table is dominated by features included in every plan, making genuine trade-offs hard to scan.
action: Add a reversible “Show differences only” control that filters identical rows while preserving plan headings, prices and critical terms. Show how many shared features are hidden and keep a one-step route to the full comparison.
mechanism: Removing redundant information may reduce comparison effort.
guardrail: Treat blank, limited and unavailable as distinct values; never filter out a material exclusion or a conditional entitlement.
measure: Comparison-to-paid completion; mistaken-plan selections.

title: Separate paid editors from free collaborators
trigger: Teams hesitate because they assume every person who views or comments requires a full paid seat.
action: Where the existing offer allows it, show distinct editor, viewer and guest roles with their prices and permissions. Provide a small team example combining the roles that the actual billing system supports.
mechanism: A clearer participation model may reduce perceived team cost and adoption resistance.
guardrail: Verify role limits, guest restrictions and conversion to paid seats; changing who pays requires commercial approval.
measure: Team purchases; seat surprises and collaboration-related support.

title: Give the free tier a clear durable job
trigger: A freemium plan feels like an unusable teaser, or its boundaries make the paid plans difficult to understand.
action: Define a sustainable recurring job the free plan genuinely completes, then explain the specific capacity or workflow that paid plans unlock. Present free and paid as useful options with clear boundaries.
mechanism: Credible free value may support learning and make the reason to pay more concrete.
guardrail: Treat entitlement changes as commercial; model service cost and avoid making essential user data inaccessible at the boundary.
measure: Activated free accounts converting to paid; service cost and free-tier abandonment.

title: Unbundle a costly specialist capability
trigger: A minority feature inflates the price of every package and blocks buyers who do not need it.
action: Propose an optional specialist module with a clear standalone job and price, while preserving a complete core workflow. Show a configured total when the module is selected so the revised package is easy to evaluate.
mechanism: A closer fit between price and required capability may reduce rejection of an oversized offer.
guardrail: Review margin, support complexity and existing commitments; do not remove promised features from current customers without an authorized migration.
measure: Paid conversion and contribution; add-on confusion and feature-loss complaints.

title: Bundle capabilities that complete one job
trigger: Buyers must assemble several separately priced modules to achieve a common, clearly defined outcome.
action: Propose a job-based bundle that includes the required modules together, and display its full contents and actual saving against buying those same modules separately. Keep a la carte options visible where they remain suitable.
mechanism: A coherent package may reduce assembly effort and make the outcome feel attainable.
guardrail: Use a real standalone comparison; assess cannibalization and do not add unwanted modules just to inflate apparent value.
measure: Bundle purchases and contribution; unused-module complaints.

title: Offer a practical small-team starting package
trigger: A team product’s minimum purchase is built for a larger department, leaving small groups unable to start economically.
action: Propose a bounded starter workspace with enough collaborators and shared functionality to complete a real team task. Show the actual starting total and a clear path for adding capacity later.
mechanism: A credible smaller commitment may make team evaluation and adoption easier.
guardrail: Model support and infrastructure costs; do not create a nominal team plan that still requires immediate add-ons to function.
measure: Small-team paid activation; early expansion and support cost.

title: Make the next growth band predictable
trigger: Buyers fear that adding a few colleagues or projects will unexpectedly force a much larger package.
action: Show the real thresholds between capacity bands and a worked growth example. Where the jump is unjustified, propose an intermediate band or additive capacity option with explicit economics and migration behavior.
mechanism: A predictable growth path may reduce fear of future lock-in or price cliffs.
guardrail: Changing bands is commercial; verify boundary calculations, grandfathering and whether usage triggers automatic charges or only prompts a choice.
measure: Paid conversion near thresholds; threshold-related churn and disputes.

title: Separate enterprise service from basic usefulness
trigger: The enterprise column lists vague “custom” benefits, making self-serve buyers unsure whether lower tiers are complete.
action: State the verified service or organizational requirements that justify enterprise—such as a specific support arrangement or deployment option—and explicitly identify the complete workflows available self-serve.
mechanism: Clear boundaries may reassure smaller buyers while qualifying larger ones.
guardrail: Do not imply unsupported procurement, compliance or service guarantees; identify capabilities that require a separate agreement.
measure: Self-serve purchases and qualified enterprise opportunities; misrouted leads.

title: Remove accidental holes in the plan ladder
trigger: A middle tier omits a capability included below it, or similar features change names and appear unrelated.
action: Audit the real entitlement map and make the ladder understandable. Clarify intentional trade-offs in the comparison; propose correcting accidental package holes instead of letting inconsistent labels imply a smooth upgrade.
mechanism: A consistent mental model may make higher-tier choices easier to trust.
guardrail: Do not silently change entitlement enforcement; separate presentation repairs from commercially approved package changes.
measure: Paid plan selection; unexpected feature-loss tickets and downgrades.

title: Separate genuinely different product families
trigger: One pricing table mixes offers for unrelated jobs, forcing visitors to compare dimensions that do not apply to them.
action: Group the real offers into clearly labeled product families with a reversible selector and a short explanation of each job. Keep cross-family differences and any required base subscription explicit.
mechanism: Removing irrelevant alternatives may reduce decision complexity.
guardrail: Do not hide a cheaper suitable offer or infer family from sensitive traits; preserve direct links to each complete catalog view.
measure: Qualified purchase completion; family-switching and wrong-product refunds.

title: Make capacity rollover part of the package
trigger: Buyers with uneven workloads reject a rigid allowance because they expect to waste paid capacity in quiet periods.
action: Model a commercially sustainable rollover option with a clear expiry, cap and consumption order. Present it as a real package property, including how it behaves on cancellation or plan changes.
mechanism: A better match to uneven usage may reduce anticipated waste.
guardrail: Requires commercial and billing work; verify unit economics, expiry communication and entitlement accounting before publishing the benefit.
measure: Paid conversion among variable-use buyers; liability, unused balances and support.

title: Merge packages with no meaningful distinction
trigger: Several tiers differ only in minor details and buyers repeatedly ask which one they should choose.
action: Use actual purchase and objection evidence to identify redundant offers. Propose merging a pair or moving a minor differentiator to an option, retaining meaningful capacity and service distinctions.
mechanism: Fewer redundant choices may reduce comparison work without removing useful variety.
guardrail: Do not assume a fixed ideal plan count; review customer contracts, migration effects and segments that rely on the distinction.
measure: Paid selection completion; segment loss and contribution changes.

title: Distinguish active inventory from monthly usage
trigger: A plan’s quantity label makes buyers unsure whether it counts stored items, simultaneous work or consumption during a period.
action: Name the exact entitlement in the card and matrix: “20 active projects at once,” “200 exports per calendar month,” or the verified equivalent. Explain what frees capacity and what resets.
mechanism: A concrete accounting model may make the package easier to fit to real work.
guardrail: Verify enforcement and reset behavior; do not turn an active-item limit into a recurring allowance or imply rollover.
measure: Paid conversion; quota misunderstandings and blocked-work complaints.

title: Choose a value metric buyers can forecast
trigger: The billing unit tracks internal compute cost but customers cannot predict it or connect it to useful value.
action: Propose a better-understood billable unit or a bounded base-plus-usage package using actual workload and cost data. Prototype the comparison against the current unit before changing the catalog.
mechanism: A predictable value metric may reduce purchase uncertainty and make expansion feel proportionate.
guardrail: Treat this as commercial and billing design; verify metering, cost exposure, misuse and migration rather than merely renaming the same unit.
measure: Qualified purchases and contribution; bill variance and metering disputes.

title: Allow mixed paid capability levels within teams
trigger: An entire team must buy the advanced tier even though only a few members need its specialist capabilities.
action: Propose a mixed paid-seat package that keeps a complete shared workflow while assigning advanced individual capabilities only to members who need them. Show a realistic team configuration and the total compared with an all-advanced purchase.
mechanism: A closer match between capability and need may reduce rejection of an oversized team commitment.
guardrail: Requires commercial approval and entitlement/provider feasibility; distinguish individual features from workspace-wide benefits and assess arbitrage, support complexity and margin.
measure: Team paid adoption and contribution; entitlement confusion and mixed-seat support.
